question.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066449/assets/34f6562d5a661d3a58755622571f50752aefa11c8e58b85dad5c70b13c179746.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta +1}$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )={e}^{\theta +1}$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{({e}^{\theta +1})}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2\theta +2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\theta +2}{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2\pi +2}-{e}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2}({e}^{2\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$
